A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) from the atria makes the kidneys lose more sodium and water, lowering blood volume and blood pressure.

A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.q: Which enzyme, found mostly in the lungs, converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II?
A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), found mostly in the lungs, converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II, which constricts vessels and triggers aldosterone release.

A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.q: Which male gland surrounds the urethra just below the urinary bladder?
A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: The prostate surrounds the urethra just below the bladder and adds a milky, slightly acidic fluid containing enzymes such as PSA.

A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.q: In which structure do sperm mature and remain stored before ejaculation?
A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: Sperm made in the seminiferous tubules move to the epididymis, where they mature and are stored.

A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.q: Which hypothalamic hormone triggers the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH?
A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete FSH and LH.

A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.q: Which anterior pituitary hormone stimulates ovarian follicles to grow early in the cycle?
A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) stimulates follicle growth in the follicular phase.

A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.q: Which hormone stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk?
A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary drives milk production; oxytocin causes milk ejection.

A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.q: Which layer of the uterine wall has a functional layer that is shed during menstruation?
A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: The endometrium lines the uterus; its functional layer is shed each menstrual phase and rebuilt in the proliferative phase.

A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.q: Which hormone do home pregnancy tests detect?
A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: Pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), secreted by the trophoblast after implantation; it keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone.

A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.q: Through the end of which week after fertilization is the developing human called an embryo?
A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: The embryonic period runs through week 8, while the organ systems form; from week 9 to birth the developing human is a fetus.

A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.q: Which membrane surrounds the fetus and holds the fluid that cushions it?
A&P: Digestive, Urinary & Reproductive.w: The amnion encloses the fetus in amniotic fluid, which cushions it and helps keep its temperature steady.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which bone cells build new bone by secreting osteoid matrix?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Osteoblasts build bone (blasts build, clasts carve). Once trapped in the matrix they become osteocytes.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: What are the tiny channels that link osteocytes in neighboring lacunae?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Canaliculi are tiny channels that connect lacunae, letting osteocytes exchange nutrients and wastes.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: In an adult, where is most red bone marrow found?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.a: Spongy bone of flat bones and vertebrae
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Adult red marrow (hematopoiesis) is in spongy bone: flat bones such as the sternum and hip bones, vertebrae and the epiphyses of the femur and humerus.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which bone does not articulate with any other bone?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The hyoid, in the neck, is held in place by muscles and ligaments and forms no joint with another bone.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which vertebra has a dens that lets the head rotate from side to side?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The axis (C2) has the dens, a peg the atlas pivots around, allowing the side-to-side "no" rotation.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which is the longest and strongest bone in the human body?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which muscle group flexes the knee and extends the hip?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus) flex the knee and extend the hip.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which muscle closes the jaw during chewing?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The masseter elevates the mandible, closing the jaw for chewing.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: What is the role of a muscle that opposes the prime mover by relaxing and stretching?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The antagonist opposes the agonist's action; it relaxes and stretches while the agonist contracts.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: What is the contractile unit of a myofibril, running from one Z disc to the next?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The sarcomere, from Z disc to Z disc, is the basic contractile unit of skeletal muscle.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: During the cross-bridge cycle, what happens when ATP binds a myosin head?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: ATP binding releases the myosin head from actin; without ATP the heads stay attached (rigor mortis).

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.a: One motor neuron and all the fibers it supplies
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: A motor unit is a single motor neuron plus every muscle fiber it innervates; recruiting more units increases force.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which protein makes keratinocytes tough and water-resistant?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Keratin is the tough, waterproofing protein that fills keratinocytes and the dead cells of the stratum corneum.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which layer beneath the dermis stores fat and is the site of subcutaneous injections?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) is adipose and areolar tissue that insulates, stores energy and anchors the skin.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which receptors in the dermal papillae detect light touch?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Meissner (tactile) corpuscles sit in the dermal papillae of the papillary layer and detect light touch.

Biology.q: What term names a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring?
Biology.w: A species is a group whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

Biology.q: Which domain includes all organisms whose cells have a nucleus?
Biology.w: Eukarya contains every eukaryote: protists, fungi, plants and animals.

Biology.q: What is an organism that makes its own food from light or chemical energy called?
Biology.w: An autotroph makes its own food by photosynthesis or chemosynthesis.

Biology.q: In evolutionary biology, what does fitness mean?
Biology.w: Fitness = reproductive success, the number of surviving, fertile offspring left.

Biology.q: What term describes structures with the same basic anatomy but different functions, such as a human arm and a bat wing?
Biology.w: Homologous structures share an underlying structure inherited from a common ancestor.

Biology.q: What is the original source of new alleles in a population?
Biology.w: Mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles; other processes sort or reshuffle existing ones.

Biology.q: What type of bond forms between neighboring water molecules?
Biology.w: Hydrogen bonds link the partially positive H of one water molecule to the partially negative O of another.

Biology.q: Which term describes water molecules sticking to one another?
Biology.w: Cohesion is water-to-water attraction; it produces surface tension.

Biology.q: Which term describes substances, such as oils, that do not dissolve in water?
Biology.w: Hydrophobic (water-fearing) substances are nonpolar and do not dissolve in water.

Biology.q: Which class of macromolecule provides the most energy per gram, about 9 kcal?
Biology.w: Lipids store about 9 kcal/g; carbohydrates and proteins give about 4 kcal/g.

Biology.q: What are the monomers of proteins?
Biology.w: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

Biology.q: Which polysaccharide forms plant cell walls and cannot be digested by humans?
Biology.w: Cellulose builds plant cell walls; humans lack the enzyme to digest it, so it acts as dietary fiber.

Biology.q: What role do enzymes play in the body?
Biology.w: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they lower activation energy and are not used up.

Biology.q: Which enzyme digests the milk sugar lactose?
Biology.w: Enzyme names often end in -ase and name the substrate: lactase digests lactose.

Biology.q: What are inorganic enzyme helpers, such as Mg2+ and Zn2+ ions, called?
Biology.w: Cofactors are inorganic helpers such as metal ions; coenzymes are organic helpers, often from vitamins.

Biology.q: Which type of cell lacks a membrane-bound nucleus?
Biology.w: Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) keep their DNA in a nucleoid region with no nuclear membrane.

Biology.q: What is the main structural material of a plant cell wall?
Biology.w: Plant cell walls are built from the polysaccharide cellulose.

Biology.q: Which statement is one of the three tenets of cell theory?
Biology.a: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
Biology.w: Cell theory: all living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; all cells come from pre-existing cells.

Biology.q: Which cell structure is the site of protein synthesis?
Biology.w: Ribosomes translate mRNA into protein, free in the cytoplasm or bound to rough ER.

Biology.q: Which organelle uses catalase to convert hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen?
Biology.w: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and toxins, and their catalase turns H₂O₂ into water and O₂.

Biology.q: Which plant cell structure stores water and maintains turgor pressure?
Biology.w: The large central vacuole stores water, ions and wastes and keeps the cell turgid.

Biology.q: During osmosis, water moves toward which region?
Biology.a: The region of higher solute concentration
Biology.w: Water moves from lower solute (higher water) concentration to higher solute (lower water) concentration.

Biology.q: What happens to a red blood cell placed in a hypotonic solution?
Biology.w: Less solute outside means water enters by osmosis, so the cell swells and may lyse (hemolysis).

Biology.q: Which transport process moves a substance against its concentration gradient?
Biology.w: Active transport uses ATP and carrier proteins (pumps) to move substances from low to high concentration.

Biology.q: In which phase of mitosis do chromosomes line up at the metaphase plate?
Biology.w: Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the cell equator (metaphase plate).

Biology.q: How many chromosomes are in a normal human egg or sperm cell?
Biology.w: Gametes are haploid (n): 23 chromosomes, half the diploid 46.

Biology.q: What does meiosis produce from one diploid parent cell?
Biology.w: Meiosis has two divisions and yields four genetically different haploid cells.

Biology.q: Where in the cell does glycolysis take place?
Biology.w: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen.

Biology.q: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
Biology.w: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP per glucose (it uses 2 and makes 4).

Biology.q: Which molecule is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain?
Biology.w: Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the chain and combines with H+ to form water.

Biology.q: Which molecule is the source of the oxygen gas released in photosynthesis?
Biology.w: Water is split in the light-dependent reactions, releasing O₂.

Biology.q: In which part of the chloroplast does the Calvin cycle occur?
Biology.w: The Calvin cycle runs in the stroma, the fluid around the thylakoids.

Biology.q: Which green pigment absorbs most of the light used in photosynthesis?
Biology.w: Chlorophyll, in the thylakoid membranes, absorbs mainly red and blue light.

Biology.q: In double-stranded DNA, adenine pairs with which base?
Biology.w: A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds); G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds).

Biology.q: Which sugar is found in RNA nucleotides?
Biology.w: RNA contains ribose; DNA contains deoxyribose.

Biology.q: In eukaryotic cells, DNA wraps around which proteins to form chromatin?
Biology.w: DNA wraps around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which pack into chromatin and chromosomes.

Biology.q: How many mRNA bases make up one codon?
Biology.w: A codon is a triplet: 3 bases code for 1 amino acid.

Biology.q: Which mRNA codon is the start codon for translation?
Biology.w: AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine.

Biology.q: Where in a eukaryotic cell does translation take place?
Biology.w: Translation happens at ribosomes, free in the cytoplasm or on the rough ER.

Biology.q: What phenotype ratio does a monohybrid cross Aa x Aa produce, with complete dominance?
Biology.w: Aa x Aa gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotypes (genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa).

Biology.q: What term describes an individual with two identical alleles for a gene, such as BB or bb?
Biology.w: Homozygous = two identical alleles (BB or bb).

Biology.q: What phenotype ratio does the dihybrid cross AaBb x AaBb produce, with complete dominance?
Biology.w: Two independently assorting heterozygous genes give 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

Biology.q: Type AB blood, in which both A and B antigens are expressed, is an example of which inheritance pattern?
Biology.w: IA and IB are codominant: both are fully expressed in an IAIB person.

Biology.q: Which genotype gives type O blood?
Biology.w: i is recessive to IA and IB, so type O requires ii.

Biology.q: Pink snapdragons (RW) are crossed with each other. What phenotype ratio do the offspring show?
Biology.w: With incomplete dominance the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio: 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW.

Chemistry.q: What is the phase change from a gas directly to a solid called?
Chemistry.w: Deposition is gas to solid, as when frost forms; it releases heat.

Chemistry.q: At sea level (1 atm), at what temperature does pure water boil?
Chemistry.w: Pure water boils at 100 °C, 212 °F or 373 K at 1 atm.

Chemistry.q: Boyle's law relates which two quantities of a gas at constant temperature?
Chemistry.w: Boyle's law: P1V1 = P2V2; pressure and volume are inversely related.

Chemistry.q: What is the formula for density?
Chemistry.w: Density = mass / volume, often in g/mL or g/cm³.

Chemistry.q: Flammability is an example of which kind of property?
Chemistry.w: Flammability describes the ability to react (burn) and form new substances, so it is a chemical property.

Chemistry.q: Which of these is a compound?
Chemistry.w: Sodium chloride is two elements chemically combined in a fixed 1:1 ratio, which makes it a compound.

Chemistry.q: What does the mass number of an atom count?
Chemistry.w: Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons, the particles in the nucleus. Neutrons = A - Z.

Chemistry.q: Which scientist discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model?
Chemistry.w: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron and pictured it embedded in a positive sphere (plum pudding).

Chemistry.q: Isotopes of the same element differ in their number of which particle?
Chemistry.w: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ.

Chemistry.q: Elements in the same group (column) of the periodic table have the same number of what?
Chemistry.w: A group shares the same number of valence electrons, which gives its elements similar chemical properties.

Chemistry.q: What is the maximum number of electrons the first electron shell can hold?
Chemistry.w: Shell capacity is 2n squared: the first shell holds 2, the second 8 and the third 18.

Chemistry.q: Which group of the periodic table contains the noble gases?
Chemistry.w: Group 18 (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) has full outer shells, making these gases very unreactive.

Chemistry.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
Chemistry.w: Fluorine, at the upper right of the table (excluding noble gases), is the most electronegative element.

Chemistry.q: Moving down a group, how does atomic radius change?
Chemistry.w: Each step down a group adds an occupied electron shell, so atoms get larger.

Chemistry.q: Which family contains the most reactive metals?
Chemistry.w: Alkali metals have one valence electron that is easily lost, making them the most reactive metals.

Chemistry.q: What is an alpha particle?
Chemistry.w: An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons, a helium-4 nucleus, with a 2+ charge.

Chemistry.q: Which nuclear process splits a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei?
Chemistry.w: Fission splits a heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235) into smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons.

Chemistry.q: What fraction of a radioactive sample remains after 3 half-lives?
Chemistry.w: Each half-life halves what is left: 1 → 1/2 → 1/4 → 1/8.

Chemistry.q: In a covalent bond, what do the atoms do with electrons?
Chemistry.w: Covalent bonds form when atoms, usually nonmetals, share pairs of electrons.

Chemistry.q: A hydrogen bond forms when hydrogen is bonded to which atoms?
Chemistry.w: Hydrogen bonds need hydrogen attached to a highly electronegative N, O or F atom.

Chemistry.q: Between two carbon atoms, which covalent bond is the strongest and shortest?
Chemistry.w: Bond strength rises from single to double to triple, and triple bonds are the shortest.

Chemistry.q: When you balance a chemical equation, which numbers may you change?
Chemistry.w: Balance with coefficients. Changing a subscript changes the substance itself.

Chemistry.q: Which law requires chemical equations to be balanced?
Chemistry.w: Mass (and so every atom) is conserved in a chemical reaction.

Chemistry.q: How many oxygen atoms are in 3 H₂SO₄?
Chemistry.w: Each H₂SO₄ has 4 O; 3 × 4 = 12.

Chemistry.q: In a redox reaction, what does oxidation mean?
Chemistry.w: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain (OIL RIG).

Chemistry.q: Which pattern represents a synthesis reaction?
Chemistry.w: In synthesis, two or more reactants combine into a single product.

Chemistry.q: What are the products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
Chemistry.w: A hydrocarbon burned in enough oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water, plus energy.

Chemistry.q: At chemical equilibrium, how do the forward and reverse reaction rates compare?
Chemistry.w: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant.

Chemistry.q: What is activation energy?
Chemistry.a: The minimum energy needed to start a reaction
Chemistry.w: Activation energy is the energy barrier colliding particles must overcome for a reaction to occur.

Chemistry.q: How does a catalyst speed up a chemical reaction?
Chemistry.w: A catalyst provides a pathway with a lower activation energy and is not used up.

Chemistry.q: About how many particles are in one mole of a substance?
Chemistry.w: Avogadro's number: 1 mol = 6.02 × 10²³ particles.

Chemistry.q: To convert a mass in grams to moles, what do you do?
Chemistry.w: moles = grams ÷ molar mass (g/mol).

Chemistry.q: In a balanced equation, where does a mole ratio come from?
Chemistry.w: Coefficients give the mole ratio between substances.

Chemistry.q: In salt water, which substance is the solvent?
Chemistry.w: The solvent does the dissolving and is present in the larger amount: water.

Chemistry.q: Molarity is defined as moles of solute per what?
Chemistry.w: Molarity (M) = moles of solute / liters of solution.

Chemistry.q: As temperature rises, what happens to the solubility of most solids in water?
Chemistry.w: Most solid solutes become more soluble as temperature rises; gases do the opposite.

Chemistry.q: At 25 °C, what pH value is neutral?
Chemistry.w: Pure water at 25 °C has pH 7: [H⁺] = [OH⁻].

Chemistry.q: In the Bronsted-Lowry definition, what is an acid?
Chemistry.w: A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton (H⁺); a base accepts one.

Chemistry.q: Which ion does an Arrhenius base release in water?
Chemistry.w: An Arrhenius base releases hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in water.

Physics.q: Which of these quantities is a vector?
Physics.w: Velocity has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector.

Physics.q: What does the slope of a velocity-time graph represent?
Physics.w: Slope = change in velocity / change in time = acceleration.

Physics.q: A car rounds a curve at a steady 20 m/s. Is it accelerating?
Physics.w: Acceleration is any change in velocity, including a change in direction. On a curve the direction changes, so the car accelerates.

Physics.q: A falling skydiver reaches terminal velocity when:
Physics.w: At terminal velocity drag balances weight, so the net force and the acceleration are both zero and the speed stays constant.

Physics.q: Ignoring air resistance, what is the acceleration of any freely falling object near Earth's surface?
Physics.w: All freely falling objects accelerate downward at g, about 9.8 m/s², whatever their mass.

Physics.q: Ignoring air resistance, which launch angle gives a projectile the greatest range on level ground?
Physics.w: On level ground with no air resistance, range is greatest at a 45° launch angle.

Physics.q: What is the SI unit of force?
Physics.w: Force is measured in newtons: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s², from F = m a.

Physics.q: Which property measures an object's inertia?
Physics.w: Mass is the measure of inertia: the more mass, the harder it is to change the object's motion.

Physics.q: On a level floor with no other vertical forces, the normal force on a resting box equals:
Physics.w: The normal force balances the weight, so on a level surface with no other vertical forces they are equal.

Physics.q: Which formula gives an object's momentum?
Physics.w: Momentum = mass x velocity, p = m v, in kg·m/s.

Physics.q: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects:
Physics.a: stick together and move as one
Physics.w: Perfectly inelastic means the objects stick together; momentum is conserved and the kinetic energy loss is greatest.

Physics.q: Impulse is equal to:
Physics.w: Impulse J = F t = change in momentum (N·s = kg·m/s).

Physics.q: A spinning figure skater pulls her arms in close to her body. What happens to her rate of spin?
Physics.w: Pulling mass closer to the axis lowers rotational inertia; angular momentum is conserved, so she spins faster.

Physics.q: Torque, with the force applied perpendicular to the lever arm, is:
Physics.w: Torque = lever-arm distance x perpendicular force, τ = r F, in N·m.

Physics.q: How does the gravitational force between two masses change with the distance r between their centers?
Physics.w: Universal gravitation is inverse-square: F is proportional to 1/r².

Physics.q: Compared with lifting a load straight up, an ideal simple machine reduces:
Physics.w: Simple machines trade force for distance: less force over a longer distance, with the same work.

Physics.q: What is the SI unit of power?
Physics.w: Power is energy per time, measured in watts: 1 W = 1 J/s.

Physics.q: Which formula gives kinetic energy?
Physics.w: Kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x speed squared.

Physics.q: What is the SI unit of pressure?
Physics.w: Pressure = force / area, measured in pascals: 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

Physics.q: According to Archimedes' principle, the buoyant force on an object equals:
Physics.w: Buoyant force = weight of the fluid the object displaces.

Physics.q: An object floats in a fluid when its density is:
Physics.w: An object less dense than the fluid floats; a denser one sinks.

Physics.q: What does a wave carry from one place to another?
Physics.w: Waves transfer energy; the medium's particles vibrate in place and are not carried along.

Physics.q: Why can sound not travel through the vacuum of space?
Physics.w: Sound is a mechanical wave: it needs particles of a medium to pass the vibration along.

Physics.q: Sound with a frequency above the range of human hearing is called:
Physics.w: Ultrasound is above the range of human hearing; it is used in medical imaging (sonography).

Physics.q: Which effect lets an endoscope's optical fibers carry light around bends?
Physics.w: Light inside the fiber hits the boundary beyond the critical angle and is totally reflected back in.

Physics.q: A prism separates white light into a spectrum of colors by:
Physics.w: Dispersion: each color refracts by a slightly different amount, so the colors fan out.

Physics.q: Which lens is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays to a focus?
Physics.w: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges light; it corrects farsightedness.

Physics.q: Which pair of statements about electric charges is correct?
Physics.a: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract
Physics.w: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

Physics.q: Which form of Ohm's law is correct?
Physics.w: Voltage = current x resistance; so I = V / R and R = V / I.

Physics.q: In a series circuit, the current through each resistor is:
Physics.w: A series circuit has one path, so the same current flows through every part.

Physics.q: Which of these metals is ferromagnetic?
Physics.w: Iron, nickel and cobalt (and their alloys) are ferromagnetic.

Physics.q: Outside a bar magnet, magnetic field lines run:
Physics.w: Outside the magnet, field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole.

Physics.q: Two magnets are placed with their north poles facing each other. They will:
Physics.w: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
